title: Chapter 19: Bram Comes Home
content: Ruthie Pyle stands in the doorway of the Bend Diner with her hand flat on the glass and does not open it.
"He has been in here since five," she says through the door.
Wren looks past her. A man at the counter with his back to the room and his coat still on. A white pickup in the lot with Ohio plates and a dent in the tailgate the shape of a mailbox.
"Bram."
"Bram." Ruthie opens the door six inches. "Four cups of coffee and he has not ordered food. He is scaring the church crowd."
"Then let me in."
"I am letting you in. I am telling you first."
Wren goes in. The diner smells of coffee and hot grease and the wet wool of six men who have been up since four. The clock over the register says 6:52. Bram does not turn around.
She sits one stool away and puts both hands on the counter, because her hands are the part of her that will not stay still this morning.
"You drove all night."
"Nine hours. I stopped twice."
"Your brother used to say you could not get to the end of the road without stopping."
"My brother said a lot of things."
Ruthie sets a cup in front of Wren without being asked and fills it, then stands at the end of the counter with the pot in her fist. That is Ruthie saying she is not going anywhere.
Bram turns. He is twenty-seven and looks like a man who has been awake for thirty hours. He has Ade's hands, wide across the knuckles, and that is the thing she cannot stop seeing.

"He was going to come up at Christmas," he says. "He called me in August about a truck he wanted me to look at. Then he called me in October." Bram turns his cup a quarter turn. "He said the cable was down and you were rowing people across in a tin boat and taking two dollars a head like a hired man."
"I was."
"He said it like it was funny." Bram's jaw moves once. "Like a man telling you about a woman he is not done with."
Wren drinks her coffee. It is too hot and she drinks it anyway.
Then Ruthie puts the ledger down.

She does it the way she does everything, without ceremony, one palm flat on the cover. The ledger is a wide green accounts book and the columns are not accounts. Date, name, what was said. Ruthie has kept it thirty-one years. She has never once pretended it was kind.
"Page forty," Ruthie says. "You have been sitting here since five, reading the paper and asking nobody anything. So read the page."
"Why."
"Because you drove nine hours to be angry at the wrong person and I have a business to run."
Bram does not touch the book. Ruthie taps it once with one finger, the way she taps a grill that is not hot enough.
He reads.

Wren cannot see the page from where she sits. She does not need to. She has heard the sentence twice already, once from a man buying a coffee and once from a woman who has crossed with her four times and would not meet her eye on the fifth.
Bram's finger stops. He reads the line again, moving his lips very slightly, which is what people do when a sentence is heavier than they expected.
Then he looks up and asks her the question as though it were his own.
"Did you take him out in a storm for two dollars a head."
The diner gets quiet in the way rooms get quiet when the men at the far table decide to be interested in their plates.
"No," Wren says. It is true and it is not an answer and they both know it.
"Did you take him out."
"Yes."
"For two dollars a head."
She reaches into the canvas bag on the floor and takes out the log.

It is a hardbound book the size of a church Bible, and the cover has gone soft at the corners from fifty-one years of hands. She has carried it for nine days. There is a hole in the wall of the ferry house where its shelf used to be and she has not fixed the hole.
She sets it on the counter between them and opens it to a date.
"You want the answer," she says. "It is in the book. You have three hours. I have to be at the landing at ten."
He does not read it like a man reading evidence. He reads it like a man reading a letter that has been held at the post office for a year.
Wren goes out at seven and pumps the bilge and comes back. The mail truck comes. The school bus stops and lets off four kids who look at the pickup, then at the window, then walk faster.

At eight the church crowd leaves. Two of the men at the far table put money on the counter for her coffee, which has never happened before, and one of them does it without looking at her, which is the only way it could have happened.
Ruthie flips eggs and says, to nobody, "Nine days."
It is nine days since the water. Ruthie counts things out loud the way other people pray, and Wren has stopped correcting her, because the count is the only thing in this diner that is not for sale.

The nine days since the water have a shape she can feel from the outside. Half the town says her name when she comes into a room. The other half stops saying it. The ones who stop are worse, because they watch her hands, as if the water might still be on them.
At 8:40 Bram asks, without lifting his head, "What is the circle in the margin."
"Fare waived."
"Who waives a fare."
"He did. Children. Anybody who had nothing. The priest, who had plenty."
"What is the little number."
"The crossing number. He numbered all of them. The last one had five figures in it, and he was proud of that number and would not say so."
Bram turns pages. His finger walks down the right-hand column, where the deckhand is written, and stops.
"He wrote him in."
"Every day he worked."
"He wrote him in a lot."
"He did not write many words in his life," Wren says. "He wrote that name a few thousand times and then he stopped counting, because it was his book and he already knew it."
Bram's throat moves. He turns the page and finds the name again, and again, four letters in the same square hand going down the years like fence posts every twenty feet.

She watches him find it, and she thinks about a Sunday in June, the two of them at the landing with the ferry tied up and the wind coming down the river and nothing to do. He asked her whether she was ever going to say something to him. She said something about the river. He laughed, and put his boot up on the piling, and let it go, and that was the last honest thing that passed between them. She has thought about it every day since June, and every hour since the twenty-second, which is not the same as grief and is doing the work of it.
At 9:20 he reaches October.

She knows the page before he gets to it. She can see the ink change from the side. Elias wrote with a fountain pen and a light hand. Wren writes with a ballpoint and presses too hard, and the storm page has a dent in it you can feel from the other side of the paper.
Nine names. The child first, because the child was in the bow. A time beside each one. The fare column empty.
Bram puts his finger on the empty column and leaves it there.
"Nobody paid."
"Nobody pays in weather."
"Not one of them."
"The child's mother tried. I put it back in her coat pocket at the landing and she cried about that, not about the water."
"Which one was the child."
"The one in the bow. She was six and she had a plastic horse in her fist, and she did not let go of it, not on the boat and not on the gravel and not in the ambulance."
Bram looks at the page a long time. "Six."
"Six."
He reads down. The tenth line says A. Kessler, 7:20 p.m. There is nothing after it. There is a smudge where she rested her hand.
He sits with that a while. Ruthie fills his cup and he does not drink it.
Then he closes the book, squares it with the edge of the counter, and puts both palms flat on the cover the way a man holds down a table that is about to move.
"He was a good deckhand," he says.
"He was better than good."

"He was thirty-one years old and he died getting a child out of the water, and the paper said it was unrelated to gate operations." Bram says it slowly, without heat, the way a man reads a number off a bill. "I read that sentence in a parking lot in Brook Park on my lunch break."
"I know."
"You did not call me."
"I did not have your number. Ade had your number. He kept it in a drawer with a picture of your mother and a spare key to a truck he did not own anymore."
Bram's face does something and then stops doing it.
A man in a feed cap at the register says, not quite to Ruthie, "I heard she had nine in that boat."
Ruthie does not turn around. "Out."
"I am paying."
"Pay at the door and be out." She takes his two dollars and holds the door with her hip until he is through it. Then she comes back and wipes the counter in front of Bram, hard, twice.
"That one crossed with her in June," Ruthie says. "He is not a bad man. He is just a man who has not thought about it for one minute."
Bram looks at the door and then at the log and then at his own hands.
"There is a horn," he says. "At the gate. There is supposed to be a horn."
"There is supposed to be a lot of things."
"Then what are you doing." He nods at the book. "You filed papers. Forty of them, fifty, I do not know. What is that going to do."
"Forty-one."
"Forty-one." He says the number back to her like a man testing a coin. "And what does it get you."

"A docket that moves, because the county opens one in the order things come in, and a docket with a name on it moves faster than a drawer." She puts her hand flat on the counter. "I want one word on one certificate. Drowned. Not pending. Not misadventure. Drowned."
"That is all."
"That is all."
He looks at her for a long moment, and she can see him deciding whether she is a woman with a plan or a woman who has been in the water too long.
Then he says, "How many names are pending."
"Forty-one."
He turns the book around on the counter, opens it to October, and puts his finger on the tenth line.
"Forty-two now."
highlight: Bram comes home, asks Wren if she killed his brother, then reads the log and finds the line that makes forty-two.
